evidence.speaker: Henry Morgenthau
evidence.context: Attribution retained from the current case text: U.S. Ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, 1918.

chronology.text: Armenian soldiers in the Ottoman army are disarmed, demobilized, and largely executed.

Hundreds of Armenian intellectuals, community leaders, and professionals are arrested in Constantinople (Istanbul) and subsequently executed or deported, marking the widely recognized start of the genocide.

Mass deportations (death marches) begin from eastern Anatolia, extending to other Armenian-populated regions. Armenians are forced to march into the Syrian Desert (Deir ez-Zor), often without food, water, or protection, facing starvation, disease, and attacks.

Massacres continue across various regions, perpetrated by Ottoman soldiers, gendarmerie, Kurdish irregulars, and local gangs. Concentration camps are established in the desert, where survivors of the marches perish from starvation and disease.

With the end of WWI and the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, the violence largely subsides, but the vast majority of the Armenian population within the Ottoman Empire has been annihilated or dispersed.

duration.note: Judgement call. The Holodomor can be measured as the full 1932–1933 famine or as the months of peak mortality in the first half of 1933. This record uses the full span — from the August 1932 Law of Spikelets to the end of the summer of 1933 — because the engineered character of the famine lies in the procurement quotas and the border blockade, not only in when people died. Peak mortality alone would be roughly a quarter as long.

argumentRole.text: Coercive state policy and mass starvation as a case of political violence against a population.

evidence.speaker: Gareth Jones
evidence.context: Attribution retained from the current case text: press statement after walking through rural Ukraine, March 1933.

chronology.text: Intensified collectivization drives in Ukraine, met with significant peasant resistance, including destruction of crops and livestock rather than surrendering them to collective farms.
The “Law of Spikelets” (Law on the Safeguarding of Socialist Property) is enacted, making theft of collective farm property, even a few stalks of grain, punishable by death or long prison sentences.

Grain procurement quotas for Ukraine are drastically increased, often exceeding the total harvest. Brigades search homes and confiscate all foodstuffs, including seeds and previously hidden provisions.
Internal passports are introduced, and border blockades are established around Ukraine to prevent starving peasants from leaving to seek food elsewhere.
The famine reaches its peak, with millions dying from starvation and associated diseases. Reports of cannibalism become increasingly common.
Harvest improves due to good weather and reduced quotas after the population has been decimated, but the effects linger for years.

evidence.context: Attribution retained from the current case text: diary entry, 16 December 1937.

chronology.text: Second Sino-Japanese War begins.
Shanghai falls to Japanese forces after heavy fighting, preceding their advance on Nanking.
Japanese forces issue an ultimatum for Nanking’s surrender.
Japanese troops enter Nanking. Organized mass killings and atrocities begin immediately.
The peak period of the massacre and widespread atrocities, lasting approximately six weeks.
The violence begins to subside, but systematic killings and harassment continue on a smaller scale for several more weeks.

evidence.speaker: Hugh Thompson
evidence.context: Attribution retained from the current case text: U.S. Army helicopter pilot, on why he intervened.

chronology.text: Tet Offensive by North Vietnamese forces and Viet Cong intensifies the war, increasing U.S. troop frustration and aggression.
Charlie Company sustains casualties from booby traps and mines in the Quang Ngai province, fueling a desire for retaliation.
Charlie Company enters My Lai hamlet, expecting armed Viet Cong. Instead, they encounter unarmed civilians.

Soldiers systematically round up, torture, rape, and execute hundreds of unarmed civilians. Lt. William Calley orders most of the killings. Warrant Officer Hugh Thompson Jr., a helicopter pilot, intervenes to protect civilians and report the atrocities.
Elements of the company continue to destroy the village and kill survivors.
Initial military cover-up attempts.
Ron Ridenhour, a former soldier, writes to Congress, the Pentagon, and others, detailing the massacre, forcing an investigation. Seymour Hersh breaks the story to the public.
Public outrage, military investigations, and court-martials begin.

duration.note: Judgement call. Measured as the full duration of Khmer Rouge rule, 17 April 1975 to 7 January 1979, rather than as a shorter window of continuous killing. Deaths from execution, forced labour and starvation ran across the whole regime rather than in one concentrated episode, so the regime span is the measure that can be found rather than chosen.

argumentRole.text: Revolutionary state power, forced social transformation and mass killing under an all-encompassing political project.

evidence.speaker: Khmer Rouge slogan
evidence.context: Current case text describes this as a regime slogan recited to prisoners.

chronology.text: Khmer Rouge forces capture Phnom Penh, ending the civil war. Immediately begin forced evacuation of urban populations to the countryside.
Establishment of rural communes; widespread forced labor, starvation, and execution of “new people” (urbanites). Elimination of money, private property, and organized religion.

Pol Pot consolidates power; internal purges within the Khmer Rouge begin, targeting those suspected of disloyalty or “bourgeois” tendencies. Tuol Sleng (S-21) security prison becomes a major torture and execution center.
Escalation of purges and executions. Increasing border clashes with Vietnam.
Vietnam invades Cambodia to overthrow the Khmer Rouge after years of border provocations.
Vietnamese forces capture Phnom Penh, ending the Khmer Rouge regime.

evidence.speaker: Rufina Amaya (recounting her son’s words)
evidence.context: The current case text presents Amaya’s account as testimony later supported by forensic exhumation.

chronology.text: Salvadoran Civil War intensifies. U.S. military aid and training for the Salvadoran armed forces increase.
Atlacatl Battalion arrives in the vicinity of El Mozote, rounding up villagers from several hamlets and gathering them in El Mozote.

Soldiers systematically separate men, women, and children. Beginning in the early morning, they execute groups of men, then rape and execute women and girls, and finally kill the children, often by slitting their throats or machine-gunning them in groups. Homes are burned afterward.
Troops continue to sweep through nearby hamlets, perpetrating similar atrocities and destroying evidence.

Initial reports of the massacre by journalists Raymond Bonner (New York Times) and Alma Guillermoprieto (Washington Post) are published, but largely dismissed by U.S. and Salvadoran officials as FMLN propaganda.
Official cover-up and denial by both the Salvadoran and U.S. governments persist for years.
Forensic anthropologist Clyde Snow begins exhumations in El Mozote.
The UN Truth Commission for El Salvador confirms the massacre, detailing the military’s responsibility.
Salvadoran government apologizes for the massacre.
Salvadoran Supreme Court overturns an amnesty law, reopening the El Mozote case for prosecution.

evidence.speaker: Roméo Dallaire
evidence.context: Attribution retained from the current case text: UNAMIR force commander.

chronology.text: Hutu Revolution and independence from Belgium; mass exodus of Tutsis, and establishment of Hutu-dominated government.
Rwandan Civil War between the Hutu government and the Tutsi-led RPF begins. Extremist Hutu propaganda intensifies, demonizing Tutsis.
Arusha Accords signed, a power-sharing agreement between the government and RPF, viewed as a betrayal by Hutu extremists.
President Habyarimana’s plane is shot down, widely blamed on Hutu extremists eager to avoid implementing the Accords.

Genocide begins. Hutu Power factions take control, implement roadblocks, and begin systematic killings of Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana and ten Belgian UN peacekeepers are murdered.

Widespread slaughter across the country by the Rwandan Army (FAR), Presidential Guard, Gendarmerie, and civilian militias (Interahamwe, Impuzamugambi), often using machetes and clubs. UN peacekeepers are largely withdrawn.
RPF captures Kigali.
RPF gains control of the country, ending the genocide. A new government is formed, and millions of Hutus (including perpetrators) flee to Zaire (now DRC).

duration.note: Judgement call. This case is presented as the 1992–1995 Bosnian War with Srebrenica as its focal atrocity, so the duration measures the war — roughly 1,370 days — not the eight days of the Srebrenica killings in July 1995. Figure 03 compares tempo, and using the eight-day window here would set a four-year campaign of ethnic cleansing beside a single-morning massacre.

argumentRole.text: Ethnic cleansing, organized mass execution and the failure of international protection in a declared safe area.

evidence.speaker: Judge Fouad Riad
evidence.context: Attribution retained from the current case text: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, confirming the Srebrenica indictment, November 1995.

chronology.text: Bosnian War begins following Bosnia and Herzegovina’s declaration of independence. Bosnian Serb forces, supported by the Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA)/Serbia, launch offensives.
Widespread “ethnic cleansing” campaigns by Bosnian Serb forces against Bosniak and Croat populations across Bosnia, involving systematic killings, forced displacement, rape, and concentration camps.
Srebrenica is declared a UN “safe area,” but remains inadequately protected and besieged.
Bosnian Serb Army (VRS) under General Ratko Mladić launches its final offensive on Srebrenica. Dutch UN peacekeepers are overwhelmed.

Over 8,000 Bosniak men and boys from Srebrenica are systematically separated, transported, and executed by VRS forces in the surrounding areas. Mass graves are created. Women, children, and elderly are forcibly displaced.
NATO launches airstrikes against Bosnian Serb positions (Operation Deliberate Force) following the Srebrenica massacre and a market bombing in Sarajevo.
Dayton Peace Accords are signed, ending the war.
